It's widely accepted in the anthropological community that the reason we developed a large brain is that we ate animals. The original paper was the expensive tissue hypothesis by Leslie Aielo and Peter Wheeler, but it's widely accepted now.

http://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdfplus/10.1086/204350

TL;DR of the pdf - every animal of a certain size has a constant metabolic expenditure. So a 60kg primate, whether it's a human or some other 60kg primate, has the same metabolic demands (that's called Kleiber's law). So if the brain of a human is bigger than the brain of an orangutan (it is) then some other organ must be using less energy or else the total demand would be more (but it can't be according to Kleiber's law). So what organ is using less energy in a human to make up for these massive brains using a lot more energy? Answer: it's mostly the gut. And how did humans get a smaller gut? By eating a lot more animals than before.

My own addition: A classic comparison is a cow and a dog. The cow has to digest cellulose, so he needs massive gut systems to do it and they can never really stop eating for long. But a dog mostly eats meat, and his gut system is small and he eats only once or twice a day. Strangely enough, a dog and a human have almost the same gut systems in terms of sizes and functions of the various pieces.

So if I ever get a dog, he's probably going to eat what I eat. Lots of eggs, fresh meat, a little bit of liver now and then, and a lot of animal fats.
